title: Big AI Wants You to Believe It Could Destroy the World – So It Can Fill Its Pockets
author: Paris Marx
content:
_**Note from our Editor-in-Chief:** In just the last week, several [AI
researchers and executives](https://zeteo.com/p/the-ai-apocalypse-here-
are-9-ai-experts) have expressed growing concerns that AI could kill all
humans in the next decade. But should you be worried? Or, are the warnings
overblown? **Zeteo** is publishing a pair of essays from each side of this
contentious issue._

_The first,[ published yesterday](https://zeteo.com/p/how-to-stop-ai-from-
killing-humanity), was from AI researcher and author **Nate Soares,** who
argued the threat is real and we must heed the warning signs immediately. The
second, below, is from **Paris Marx,** a Canadian tech critic and host of the
acclaimed 'Tech Won't Save Us' podcast, who is skeptical about the end-of-
humanity warnings._

Artificial intelligence is out for humanity. You've probably heard we might
just have 10 years left - or at least that's what some in the tech industry
want us to believe. But should we really trust those sensationalist warnings?
I'm skeptical.

This question is in the headlines again because now former Anthropic employee
Jacob Coxon posted [a thread to X on Sept.
8](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843) claiming OpenAI and
Anthropic "are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and
gambling with our lives." In effect, Coxon
[claims](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476196791709843) the
technologies that underpin the chatbots that have quickly become ubiquitous
are getting close to improving on their own, without human oversight, and thus
are headed toward the holy grail of many AI leaders: the replication of human
intelligence inside the computer.

[Subscribe now](https://zeteo.com/subscribe)

The only problem? That artificial superintelligence might turn against its
creators - that's us humans - and engage in some theoretical effort to wipe us
out or enslave us. If you think that sounds like the plot of a blockbuster
science fiction movie, I'd say you're spot on, and that we should take the
industry's warnings with some caution rather than jumping to believe they're
the most trustworthy narrators of where the technology is heading.

Let's take a step back for a moment, and look at how we got here.
